record.paper_title: Using GANs for Sharing Networked Time Series Data: Challenges, Initial Promise, and Open Questions
record.original_question: If differential privacy is not well aligned with GAN-generated networked time-series releases, what alternative privacy metrics should be explored for this form of synthetic data sharing?

evidence.quote: More broadly, we believe there is value to exploring different privacy metrics.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the setting in which a data holder possesses a dataset of networked time series, i.e., a collection of multivariate sequences {X_i = (X_i^{(1)}, X_i^{(2)}, ..., X_i^{(T_i)})}_{i=1}^N indexed by entities in a network (each X_i^{(t)} ∈ R^d, possibly accompanied by static attributes A_i ∈ R^k). The holder wishes to release a synthetic dataset {Ŷ_j}_{j=1}^M produced by a generative adversarial network (GAN) trained on {X_i, A_i} so that downstream parties may perform analyses (e.g., distributional fidelity of marginals, autocorrelations, cross-series correlations, and rare-event statistics) without compromising the privacy of contributing entities.

Recall that a randomized release mechanism M satisfies (ε, δ)-differential privacy if for every pair of datasets D, D' differing in a single entity's record and every measurable set S of outputs, Pr[M(D) ∈ S] ≤ e^ε · Pr[M(D') ∈ S] + δ. Empirically, training GANs under (ε, δ)-DP with practically meaningful (ε, δ) typically degrades fidelity of long, high-dimensional networked time series substantially.

Problem. Propose and rigorously formalize a privacy metric P (a functional on pairs (training distribution, release mechanism)) suitable for evaluating GAN-based releases of networked time-series data, satisfying all of the following desiderata:
(a) P admits a precise mathematical definition with explicit adversarial threat model (specifying adversary knowledge, queries, and success criterion).
(b) P composes under repeated or sequential releases in a quantifiable way.
(c) P is post-processing robust: applying any data-independent function to the release does not decrease privacy as measured by P.
(d) P captures protection against the principal attacks relevant to time-series releases—membership inference, attribute inference of static attributes A_i, and trace/trajectory reconstruction of X_i—via provable reductions.
(e) P is empirically estimable from a trained GAN and a finite training set with computable confidence bounds.
(f) Under P, there exist non-trivial GAN training procedures that achieve a quantitatively meaningful privacy level while preserving utility (measured by a stated set of statistical functionals of the time series) strictly better than what is achievable under (ε, δ)-differential privacy at comparable utility.

Provide such a metric P, prove items (a)–(d), give an estimator with finite-sample guarantees for (e), and exhibit a training algorithm with a theorem establishing (f), or prove that no metric can simultaneously satisfy (a)–(f).
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction concerning alternative privacy notions for GAN-generated networked time series. Subsequent literature has proposed candidate metrics (e.g., membership-inference-based audits, attribute-inference resistance, plausible deniability, Rényi DP, f-DP, and similarity-based heuristics), but no single metric has been established as a definitive replacement for differential privacy with the stated combination of properties for time-series GANs. The general problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Auditing Differentially Private Machine Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Membership-inference-based empirical privacy auditing has been proposed as a complementary metric to DP guarantees.
status_evidence.claim: Empirical privacy metrics based on inference attacks have been proposed but do not subsume DP's formal guarantees.

status_evidence.title: Plausible Deniability for Privacy-Preserving Data Synthesis
status_evidence.snippet: Plausible deniability offers an alternative privacy definition for synthetic data release.
status_evidence.claim: Alternative formal privacy notions to DP for synthetic data exist but each has trade-offs and none is uniformly accepted as a replacement.
